questions.stem: Frank, 76, is on an ED trolley after a 30-second blackout with no warning. On examination his radial pulse is regular, large-volume and 34/min. Before you see the ECG, you want bedside evidence of AV dissociation. Which examination step should you tell the examiner you are doing next?
options: Lie and then stand him to measure postural blood pressure over 3 minutes
Perform right carotid sinus massage while watching the cardiac monitor
Inspect the JVP at 45 degrees for intermittent cannon a waves
Auscultate for an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
questions.why: In AV dissociation the right atrium sometimes contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, which produces irregular cannon a waves in the JVP. A first heart sound that varies in loudness is the matching sign on auscultation.
notes: Postural BP looks for orthostatic hypotension, not AV dissociation, and standing a patient with a pulse of 34 risks another collapse, so it is deferred.
Carotid sinus massage increases vagal tone and could cause asystole in a patient who already has severe bradycardia and pauses.
An ejection systolic murmur suggests aortic stenosis as a cause of exertional syncope, but it says nothing about whether the atria and ventricles are dissociated.

questions.stem: At 11:00, Frank, 76, has a 4-second pause on the monitor with light-headedness, and his systolic BP falls to 94. His ECG shows complete heart block with a broad escape at 30/min. Pacing pads are on and IV access is in. Electrolytes are normal. He took metoprolol 50 mg at 7 am. Which drug should be given first?
options: Atropine 0.6 mg IV, repeated as needed to a maximum of 3 mg
Glucagon 5 mg IV bolus to reverse the beta-blockade
Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 10 minutes
Adrenaline 1 mg IV bolus, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes
questions.why: Under ANZCOR, symptomatic bradycardia with adverse features (syncope, pauses, hypotension) is treated first with atropine 0.5 to 0.6 mg IV, repeated up to 3 mg. If that fails, the next steps are an isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion or transcutaneous pacing.
notes: Glucagon is for beta-blocker overdose. Frank is on a therapeutic dose, and his block is below the AV node, so beta-blockade does not explain it.
IV calcium treats hyperkalaemia or calcium channel blocker toxicity. His potassium and calcium are normal.
A 1 mg IV adrenaline bolus is the cardiac arrest dose. A patient who has a pulse needs a titrated adrenaline infusion, and only if atropine fails.

questions.stem: Frank, 76, has complete heart block on his ECG. P waves at 84/min are dissociated from a regular escape rhythm at 32/min, and the QRS is 150 ms with RBBB morphology and left axis deviation. The registrar says atropine may not lift his rate much. What is the main reason for this?
options: Atropine is broken down quickly by plasma cholinesterase in older adults
Beta blockade from metoprolol stops atropine acting at muscarinic receptors
The escape focus depends on sympathetic tone, which atropine reduces
The block is in the His-Purkinje system, which has little vagal innervation
questions.why: Atropine blocks vagal (muscarinic) input, which mainly affects the SA and AV nodes. A broad escape means the block and the escape focus are below the node, where vagal tone has little effect, so atropine often fails.
notes: Atropine is cleared mostly by the liver and kidneys, not plasma cholinesterase, and a short duration would not explain the lack of any response.
Atropine acts on muscarinic receptors whether or not beta receptors are blocked, so metoprolol does not stop it binding.
Atropine is antimuscarinic and does not reduce sympathetic tone. If anything, it lets sympathetic tone act unopposed.

questions.stem: The cardiology registrar asks whether Frank, 76, could be having an inferior MI. She points out that inferior infarction usually causes block at the AV node itself with a narrow escape, rather than the broad escape Frank has. Which artery most commonly supplies the AV node?
options: Left anterior descending artery via its septal perforator branches
Right coronary artery via the AV nodal branch at the crux
Left circumflex artery via its obtuse marginal branches
Left main coronary artery via the ramus intermedius
questions.why: In most people the circulation is right-dominant, and the AV nodal artery comes off the RCA at the crux of the heart. That is why an inferior (RCA) MI usually causes AV nodal block, which is often transient and has a narrow escape.
notes: The septal perforators of the LAD supply the bundle branches. An anterior MI therefore causes block below the node with a broad escape, not AV nodal block.
In left-dominant hearts the circumflex can supply the AV node, but through its terminal posterior branch at the crux, not through the obtuse marginals, which supply the lateral wall.
The left main divides into the LAD and circumflex, and the ramus intermedius supplies the lateral wall, not the AV node.
